questions.title: Local response, EXCEPT: it does not propagate long distances
questions.question: Regarding the local response in a nerve fibre, the following is true, EXCEPT:

options.A: it can result from application of subthreshold stimulus
options.B: it is proportional to the strength of the stimulus
options.C: it can propagate along the nerve fiber for long distance
options.D: it is accompanied by increased excitability

explanations.A: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. A subthreshold stimulus is exactly what produces a local response: it opens some sodium activation gates, partially depolarising the membrane without reaching the firing level.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. The local response is graded, so its size varies directly with the strength of the subthreshold stimulus that produces it, unlike the fixed, all-or-none action potential.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the exception (the false statement). The local response is non-propagated and fades within one to two millimetres. It does not propagate along the nerve fibre for any real distance. A true action potential, by contrast, regenerates itself node-to-node or point-to-point over the fibre's whole length, which is exactly the propagating behaviour the local response lacks.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the exception -- this statement is true. Excitability is increased during a local response, because the membrane has already moved partway toward the firing level, making a further stimulus more likely to trigger a full action potential.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the local response does NOT propagate along the nerve fibre for any real distance, unlike a true action potential.

questions.title: Local response is accompanied by increased excitability
questions.question: Local response :

options.A: is a state of passive depolarization at the anode
options.B: it is accompanied by increased excitability
options.C: it obeys all or non law
options.D: it can propagate and generate another local response within a distance of 3-4 cm

explanations.A: Incorrect. Passive depolarization at the anode describes anodal break excitation, a separate phenomenon from the general local response; the local response itself is an active, graded event driven by sodium activation-gate opening at any stimulated point, not specifically anodal.
explanations.B: Correct. The local response is accompanied by increased excitability. The partial depolarization it produces moves the membrane potential closer to the firing level. A further stimulus is then more likely to reach threshold and trigger a full action potential, which is also why rapid subthreshold stimuli can summate to threshold.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The local response specifically does NOT obey the all-or-none law -- it is graded, varying in size and duration with the stimulus strength, which is the opposite of the fixed, all-or-none action potential.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The local response does not propagate at all; it fades within one to two millimetres, nowhere near the 3-4 cm distance this option describes, and it does not generate a fresh local response further along the fibre.

questions.learning_objective: State that the local response is accompanied by increased excitability, since it moves the membrane closer to the firing level.

questions.title: Excitability decreased by a fall in extracellular potassium
questions.question: Excitability of the nerve fiber is decreased in the following condition :

options.A: a decrease in ECF Na+ concentration
options.B: a decrease in ECF K+ concentration
options.C: an increase in ECF K+ concentration

explanations.A: Incorrect. A decrease in extracellular Na+ reduces the driving force for Na+ influx during depolarization (reducing action-potential amplitude), but this is not the factor named here as decreasing baseline excitability the way potassium changes do.
explanations.B: Correct. Extracellular potassium concentration sets the resting membrane potential. A decrease in ECF K+ hyperpolarizes the membrane, moving the resting potential further away from threshold, which decreases nerve fibre excitability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An increase in ECF K+ concentration instead depolarizes the resting membrane, moving it closer to threshold, which initially increases (not decreases) excitability -- the opposite direction from what this question asks about; sustained severe hyperkalaemia can later paralyse the nerve by inactivating Na+ channels, a different, later effect.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Low extracellular calcium removes some of calcium's membrane-stabilising effect on Na+ channels, lowering the threshold and increasing, not decreasing, excitability (hypocalcaemic tetany).

questions.learning_objective: State that a decrease in extracellular potassium hyperpolarizes the nerve membrane and decreases excitability.

questions.title: Myelinated fibres conduct faster than unmyelinated fibres
questions.question: Regarding conduction of action potential along a nerve fiber:

options.A: propagation of action potential requires ATP
options.B: large myelinated nerve fibers conduct faster than unmyelinated nerve fibers
options.C: saltatory conduction is associated with slowing of action potential propagation
options.D: the action potential magnitude declines as it propagates along the nerve fiber

explanations.A: Incorrect. Propagation of a single action potential itself is driven by passive ionic current flow down the axon, not a direct ATP-consuming step; ATP is instead needed afterward, to run the Na+-K+ pump that restores the ionic gradients the many action potentials have run down.
explanations.B: Correct. Large myelinated nerve fibres conduct faster than unmyelinated fibres. In a myelinated axon the internodal membrane is insulated and only the nodes of Ranvier are exposed with voltage-gated Na+ channels, so the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction) instead of regenerating continuously along the whole membrane -- this increases conduction velocity up to fifty-fold over an unmyelinated fibre of similar diameter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Saltatory conduction is associated with speeding up, not slowing, action potential propagation -- jumping between nodes is exactly what makes myelinated conduction faster than the continuous, point-to-point conduction of an unmyelinated fibre.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The action potential does not decline in magnitude as it propagates; it is regenerated at full size at each point (or each node, in myelinated fibres) along the way, which is why it can travel the full length of a long axon without decrement.

questions.learning_objective: State that large myelinated nerve fibres conduct faster than unmyelinated fibres, as a direct consequence of saltatory conduction.
